label: frames_v1
reader: 20-year-old, Douyin, evening scroll; 38 key frames only; film is landscape and fills about 1/4 of a vertical phone screen (1920px source ~ 390pt wide, so 60px glyph ~ 12pt, 45px ~ 9pt, 32px ~ 6.5pt, 24px ~ 5pt)
why: Frame 1 gives me a weird point of view I have not seen before: 'suppose you are a 2100-year-old cypress', with a big age counter (2135 岁) and a pretty, calm illustrated temple courtyard. I do not know yet what the point is, but the second-person framing and the huge number make me curious enough to give it another few seconds. The yellow '2100多岁' is the thing my eye lands on first. What keeps me is the question 'what happened to this tree over 2100 years'. It is not an instant must-watch though: the picture is quiet and the first subtitle is cut off mid-sentence at 0.4s.
first_moment_I_got_curious: kf01 (3.6s) '相传,汉武帝种下了你' with the age counter dropping to 0 岁 and a tiny glowing sapling: I get that the counter will run as the tree lives. Real hook for me is kf04 (12.4s) '今天,你只靠一条树皮活着': the tree is nearly dead, now I want the story.
where_I_would_swipe_away: kf11-kf12 (47-53s): '汉武帝之后,又来了4位:光武帝、唐高宗、唐玄宗、宋真宗' with six round medallions. A list of emperor names plus years, labels too small to read on a phone, no story. This is where I would flick away if I am not a history person.

kf08-kf09 (29-35s): two scenes of ancient text (bamboo slips, a 水经注 page) in traditional characters that I cannot read, with the subtitle running over the top of them. It feels like homework. Only the highlighted '一个字没提种树' and '盖' keep me; I stay because kf10 pays it off.

kf05 (14s): a big title card '汉柏的孩子,去守汉武帝' plus '你 1501 岁' in the middle of the intro. The film has just started, the age jumps from 2135 to 1501, and the next scene resets me to 0 岁. It reads like a restart, I almost lose the thread. This is a soft swipe point, not a hard one.
kf13 (57.5s) and kf35 (139s): frames with no subtitle at all, just scenery and the age counter. Two or three seconds of nothing is where a thumb moves.
Length: the last frame is at 152s. Past about 100s (kf24 onward) I would need the 'only half alive' turn to be the reward; it is, so I would stay, but a lot of viewers would have left by kf12.
lines_I_did_not_understand: kf00 vs kf01: the subtitle says 2100多岁 but the counter says 2135 岁 - are those two different numbers? Small, but I notice.
kf05: 汉柏的孩子 / 1501 岁 - 'Han cypress's child' is not explained yet; why 1501? Looks like a title card dropped in too early.
kf06-kf07: '封禅' is not explained until the next line ('在山顶祭天,告诉天:天命在我'); the first line alone loses me for a second.
kf18 (72s): '他题诗问:谁是主,谁是客?' - who is host and who is guest? The tree vs the stone drawing? Vertical poem on the stele is traditional characters and tiny. I am intrigued but lost.
kf22 (89s): '对面院子里的唐槐' - suddenly a new yard and a new tree (唐槐) I was never introduced to, with a different camera and a bare tree. I do not know why we are there.
kf24-kf25: '西边那根' / '东边那根' - on a phone I do not know which trunk is east. The corner labels 西干/东干 are too small to help. Burned one is on the left, living one on the right, but nothing says that.
kf04 vs kf24-kf26: '只靠一条树皮活着' is said twice (60s earlier as the hook, then again as the explanation). Fine as a hook, but the second time I wonder if I missed something.
kf36: '它真是汉武帝种的吗?你信吗?' - after 2 minutes I still do not know what the real answer is. The only evidence given is a 'probably (盖)' from 600 years later. Do you want me to say no?
takeaway_in_my_words: There is a famous 'Han cypress' at the Dai Temple under Mount Tai that is said to be 2100+ years old and planted by Emperor Wu of Han. But the official history of Emperor Wu never mentions planting a tree, and the only claim is in a book from about 600 years later that uses the word 盖, 'probably'. The tree itself survived fires, Qing painting and stone carving, a 1928 market and soldiers cooking in the hall, and today one of its two trunks is dead and the other lives on a single 32 cm strip of bark. People collected its seeds and in 2024 sent 6 saplings to Emperor Wu's own tomb, so the tree's 'children' now guard him. And the film asks me whether I believe it.
surprise_that_stuck: '盖' just means 'probably': the entire 2100-year age rests on one hedge word in a book written 600 years later (kf09-kf10). Close second: a tree 11.5 m tall alive on a 32 cm strip of bark (kf25-kf26).
title_I_would_click: '它真是汉武帝种的吗?你信吗?' - a yes/no I can argue about, and the last frames put it right in the centre. 'The age is one word' would also work if it existed.
title_that_misleads: '汉柏的孩子,去守汉武帝' alone sounds like a fantasy/folk story title; on its own I would not know it is about a real tree with a real doubt over its age. It also spoils the 'saplings sent to the tomb' ending. As a card at 14s (kf05) it comes before I understand what a 汉柏 is.
what_I_would_comment: 盖=大概 真的绝了,2100岁全靠一个字  /  那所以到底是不是汉武帝种的啊,我选择信,反正它还活着  /  只剩32厘米树皮还在撑着11.5米,打工人本人了  /  6棵小树去守汉武帝的墓这段有点想哭

for_frames_only.what_this_says_in_5s: Pretty painted temple, one old twin-trunk cypress, big '2135 岁' counter, 'suppose you are a 2100-year-old cypress'. I get the 'you are the tree' setup. Subtitle is cut mid-sentence at this instant.
Now a bare field and tiny glowing sapling, counter at 0 岁, line says Emperor Wu planted you. Tree age counter = time machine. Clear.
Dark night, tree on fire, age counter shows '?'. 'A big fire burned you' - dramatic and clear.
Qing-era scroll with a drawn tree next to a burned trunk, 1762 乾隆, age 1871. 'Fire burned you, Qianlong painted you.' Fast but I follow.
Close-up on the two trunks, one dead and grey, one brown with a glowing line up it: 'today you live on one strip of bark'. Strong hook line, clearest image so far.
Title card: 'The Han cypress's child, go guard Emperor Wu' and '你 1501 岁'. Looks great, but I do not know what it means yet, and 1501 contradicts the 2135 I just saw.
Mount Tai, sapling, counter back to 0: 'In 110 BC Emperor Wu came to Mount Tai for the 封禅'. Time reset, clear. 封禅 jargon not yet explained.
Misty mountain top with a tiny red shrine: 'he sacrificed to heaven and said: the mandate is mine'. Nice, but the subtitle sits on top of the shrine - the only thing in the picture.

Rows of bamboo slips with tiny old characters and a dashed box '种树': 'The Book of Han records every trip but not one word about planting a tree'. I get the point from the subtitle only; the slips are decoration.

An ancient page with a red seal on '盖': 'hundreds of years later a North Wei book wrote: 盖 Han Wu planted it'. Subtitle overlaps the top of the page. Page text is unreadable on a phone but the highlighted 盖 is the cue.
Plain screen, subtitle: '盖 means probably. Your birth is a probably.' The best frame in the film: big clean text, a real surprise. Instant aha.
Two grey/black circles labelled 秦始皇 and 汉武帝 and the line 'after Emperor Wu, 4 more came:' - I do not know what the circles are (seals? coins?).
Six round jade-looking medals with four more emperor names and years (56, 666, 725, 1008). Boring list to a non-history person; the age counter 1117 does most of the work.
Tree with a bit of snow on top, no subtitle, age 1335. A pause frame; I do not know why it is here.
Two Qing-court silhouettes and a table: 'seven hundred years later Qianlong came to the Dai Temple 10 times'. Clear and nice style.
The same silhouettes with one drawing, a speech-bubble scroll of the tree: 'in 1762 he drew you'. Clear, cute.
A new stone slab appears with the tree carved on it: '1771 he carved the drawing into a stele'. Clear.
Camera closer, dotted line from the real tree to the carved tree: 'the you in the stone looks at the real you'. Poetic, clear, nice.
Vertical poem carved next to the tree; subtitle: 'He wrote a poem asking: who is host, who is guest?'. The carved poem is far too small to read, and I do not know what host and guest refer to.
Market stalls and shoppers behind the steles: '1928, the big temple behind you became a market'. Clear; the 2037 counter fits.
Soldiers around two cooking fires in the courtyard: 'in the Republic era soldiers moved into the hall and cooked'. Clear, a good visual.
Smoky haze, trees going bare: 'smoke killed dozens of thousand-year cypresses', with a small source credit. Strong line, readable; source line is tiny but I do not need it.
New scene: a big, cut-down tree on the left, soldiers still cooking: 'the sophora in the yard opposite also died in the war'. I do not know what 唐槐 or this yard is - feels like a side track.
Back to the calm courtyard, centred big yellow 'You survived.' (你活了下来。). Great emotional beat, readable at any size.
Zoomed on the trunks with the burned one fading: 'but you are actually only half alive; the west one burned to death some year'. A real twist. Clear.
Glowing strip up the living trunk with a big '32厘米': 'the east one lives on one 32 cm strip of bark'. Number is big and readable, the picture explains it.
Height bar '11.5米' next to the tree: 'that strip feeds an 11.5 m tall you'. Good scale contrast. The 32 cm vs 11.5 m pairing is a screenshot-worthy fact.
A basket of seeds under the trunks: 'people collected your seeds'. Clear but the basket is small.
Truck with six potted saplings on a road: '2024, your 6 little trees set off'. Cute, clear, a change of scene that wakes me up.
Truck approaching a big earth mound: 'to 茂陵 - Emperor Wu's tomb'. Clear.
Six... five saplings planted before the tomb mound (a sixth is fading in), three-line subtitle: 'the person who is said to have planted you'. Clear; this is where the title makes sense.
Six glowing trees, light rays, big centred line: 'two thousand years later, it is your children's turn to guard him'. The emotional peak. Readable.
Tourists with phones in the courtyard: 'now Mount Tai gets 8 million+ visits a year'. Clear.
Same scene, a camera flash: 'they came, and went away'. Clear.
Ghost-like silhouettes of visitors fading, centred yellow 'You have always been here.' (你一直在。). Nice, quiet; readable.
Night, tree lit softly, no subtitle, just age 2135. Mood frame; a pause, but fine after the strong line before it.
Centred: 'Did Emperor Wu really plant it? Do you believe it?' Back to the starting question. Big and readable.
End card: Juno logo, title again, the question again, a follow button, and a long row of sources. The button and title read; the source line is far too small.

frames.read: Pretty painted temple courtyard with a twin-trunk cypress, big '2135 岁' counter, line 'suppose you are a 2100-year-old cypress'. Setup is a you-are-the-tree POV.

frames.confusing: Subtitle says 2100多岁 while the counter says 2135 岁; sentence is cut off mid-line at this instant.

frames.read: Bare steppe, Mount Tai, glowing sapling, counter 0 岁: 'Emperor Wu planted you.' The tree-time-machine idea clicks here.
frames.readable: Subtitle readable; era label '相传 · 前110年' readable; small sub-label 汉武帝封禅泰山 not.
frames.confusing: Nothing big. Why the sapling is inside an oval glow is not clear but it looks nice.

frames.read: Night, fire climbing the tree, counter '?岁': 'A big fire burned you.'

frames.readable: Both subtitle lines readable; '1762 · 乾隆' ok.
frames.confusing: Very fast flip from fire to painting; the fire/painting pairing is not explained yet, but it sets up later.

frames.readable: Three-line subtitle readable; counter 2135 readable; '今天' label readable.

frames.readable: Title is huge and readable; '1501 岁' ok.
frames.confusing: 'Han cypress's child' unexplained; age 1501 breaks the counter I just learned; the film seems to restart.

frames.read: Back to Mount Tai, counter 0 岁: 'In 110 BC Emperor Wu came to Mount Tai for the 封禅.'

frame_overall.frame_I_would_screenshot: kf10 (39.6s): '“盖”,就是大概。你的出生,是个“大概”。' Runner-up kf26 (104s): 32厘米 vs 11.5米.
frame_overall.who_I_would_send_it_to: A friend who studies history or is into museums/ancient sites, or someone who has climbed Mount Tai; also my mum, who likes old trees. The 盖=大概 frame is the one I would send with 'the whole 2100 years is one word lol'.
frame_overall.readability_summary: Main subtitles (~12pt on phone) and centred big lines are fine. Anything at or below ~32px (corner sub-labels, medallion names/years, bottom '估算' line, source credits, carved/ancient text) is not readable on a phone; most of these carry real facts (e.g. '最后一位封禅的皇帝', '靠北面一条树皮输送养分', 西干/东干) so they should be said in the subtitle or enlarged.
